title: One good year in five
label: The numbers
lede: Sega published its results in yen for fiscal years ending March 31. The Dreamcast gave the consumer division one year of growth. It never gave it a profit.

blocks.title: Sega’s consumer product sales, fiscal 1998 to 2002
blocks.subtitle: Billions of yen, years ending March 31. This is the division that sold consoles and games.

points.title: The Saturn fades
points.text: Consumer sales of ¥114.5 billion and a company-wide net loss of ¥35.6 billion.[^1]

points.title: Launch in Japan
points.text: The Dreamcast goes on sale in November 1998. Consumer sales still fall to ¥84.7 billion.[^1]

points.title: Launch in the U.S. and Europe
points.text: 4.65 million consoles sold in the year. Sales rise 119.8% to ¥186.2 billion, with a ¥43.0 billion operating loss.[^1]

points.title: The second Christmas
points.text: 3.39 million consoles. Sales fall 37.8% and the division’s operating loss reaches ¥69.2 billion.[^2]

points.title: After the exit
points.text: Final hardware and accessory sales of ¥11.1 billion. Sega is now a publisher on other companies’ consoles.[^3]

blocks.source: Sega Enterprises annual report 2000[^1], Sega Corporation annual reports 2001 and 2002[^2][^3]. The fiscal 2002 figure is the renamed “Consumer business” segment.

blocks.title: Net sales and net loss, whole company
blocks.subtitle: Billions of yen. Sega lost money in all five years.
blocks.source: Consolidated statements in the annual reports for 2000, 2001 and 2002[^1][^2][^3]. Figures rounded from millions of yen.

blocks.title: Consoles sold, by fiscal year
blocks.subtitle: Millions of Dreamcast units, worldwide, as Sega reported them.
blocks.source: FY2000: 4.65 million in the year, “5.55 million overall”[^1]. FY1999 (0.90 million) is derived: 5.55 − 4.65. FY2001: 3.39 million[^2]. The same report gives a cumulative total of 8.20 million, which is 0.74 million less than these three bars add up to; Sega did not explain the difference.

blocks.title: Where the last full year’s consoles went
blocks.subtitle: Share of the 3.39 million consoles sold in fiscal 2001.
blocks.source: Unit sales by region from the annual report 2001[^2]. Percentages are derived from those units.

blocks.title: The second Christmas, in Sega’s own numbers

items.text: consoles sold worldwide from April to December 2000, against 4.65 million in the whole previous fiscal year[^4][^5][^1]
operating loss in consumer products in fiscal 2001, up from ¥43.0 billion[^2]
loss on writing down or disposing of inventory, “primarily Dreamcast hardware and peripherals”[^2]
cash left at March 31, 2001, down ¥60.7 billion in a year[^2]

blocks.source: Sega Corporation annual report 2001[^2]; AP and ABC News, January 31, 2001[^4][^5].

blocks.title: What Isao Okawa handed over
blocks.subtitle: Assets the chairman donated to Sega in January 2001, as itemised in the notes to the accounts. Billions of yen.

to.label: Investments in securities
to.note: Shares in other companies. Press reports named CSK, Ascii and NextCom.[^11]

blocks.source: Note 22 to the consolidated accounts, annual report 2001[^2]. Sega also took on ¥30.7 billion of liabilities with the gift and booked a net gain of ¥77.9 billion ($628.8 million at the report’s rate). The press put the gift at ¥85 billion, or about $695 million[^11]; an earlier report said $566.3 million[^10]. In fiscal 2002 Sega booked a ¥16.7 billion “loss on settlement of donated assets.”[^3]

blocks.body: How many Dreamcasts were sold in total is not settled. Sega’s 2001 annual report says 8.20 million by March 31, 2001.[^2] Adding its own yearly figures gives 8.94 million (derived).[^1][^2] Sales continued from inventory after that date and Sega did not publish a final unit count in its 2002 report.[^3] Figures of 9.13 million and 10.6 million are widely repeated; we could not trace either to a primary document and treat them as **unverified**.
